newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook -- firm on Iraqi export delay.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook -- firm on Iraqi export delay.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices were expected to sustain a firm tone this week, mainly reflecting ongoing questions about the timing of Iraqi oil exports, analysts and traders said on Monday.
The August contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) was at $19.60 a barrel at 16:51 GMT/12:52 EDT early on Monday afternoon, up 14 cents from Friday's settlement.
Iraqi envoy Abdul Amir al-Anbari said on Monday the second tranche of U.N. humanitarian oil sales is not likely to get underway until August.
The market had foreseen an early to mid-July start-up after an aid distribution plan was approved.

"It doesn't matter if it's next week or the middle of July or August, but the further away you get from the cutoff for the end of oil sales, the more oil you'll have in a short period of time," a Texas cash dealer said.
"The Iraqis are fully capable of meeting the demands for larger production, so that will keep the market on edge until the sales start," he said.
William Brown, president of consultants W.H. Brown and Co in New York, said the U.N. approval process for the aid distribution plan might hold up exports.
"I'm not sure the plan is going to be rubber stamped. There may be some items in there that will be subject to debate. There will be some give and take," he said.
Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz told Reuters on Sunday that his government had finalized a plan, but awaited a U.N. team to visit Baghdad to approve it.
Adding to the bullish fundamental picture is expected heavy oilfield maintenance in both the Norwegian and British North Sea sectors in August.

Some 7.6 million barrels, an average of 245,000 barrel per day (bpd), will be lost to the work against July output. That sum equals a shortfall of around 15 standard 500,000 barrel cargoes from the August loading program.
Last week's midyear OPEC meeting in Vienna has also given the market some background strength, analysts said.
"The OPEC meeting was positive," said Tom Bentz, head of the energy division at High Yield Analytics in New York. "That they are fed up with cheating sent the right message."
At the meeting, the 11-member group agreed to hold its production ceiling at 25.03 million bpd for another six months.
In the cash market, traders expected this week's domestic grade market to quiet considerably from normal trading levels ahead of the U.S. Independance Day holiday on July 4.

Refiner buying bolstered interest in sweet and sour barrels last week, eliminating the discount held by Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James and moving the key West Texas Sour/Midland grade into around a $1.20 discount.
LLS is now quoted around a 15-20 cents premium to the marker, gaining mainly on the lack of North Sea Brent fixtures heading to the U.S. Gulf.
"There doesn't seem to be as much Brent on its way, and that gives LLS the underpinning it currently has," said a cash trader.
